Do not separately rerun completed gates or run full tests and coverage concurrently.\n\nBefore delivery, inspect Git readiness without repeating validation:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ delivery: { prepare } }) => prepare()\n```\n\n`ready: true` means Git inspection and whitespace checks passed. It does not mean the worktree is clean, tests/CI passed, publication is authorized, or interactive acceptance happened. Review the returned Git status and both diff checks. Similarly, `delivery.format({ checkOnly: true })` returning `formatted: false` is a failed formatting check, not successful no-op work. Format only changed files. If delivery preparation exposes a change, correct it and rerun only the affected inner-loop checks before one final validation.\n\n## Verify CI\n\nAfter pushing, use the existing discovery/wait composition for the exact commit, not the newest unrelated run. Give waiting tool invocations a 300000 ms timeout; a helper's polling budget does not extend the outer tool timeout.\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ ci: { waitForCommit } }, input: { repo: string; sha: string }) =>\n waitForCommit({ ...input, runName: \"ci.yml\", raise: true })\n```\n\nUse `ci.findRun()` alone when only discovery is needed, or `ci.waitForRun()` when the exact run ID is already known. A missing run is a synchronization/trigger problem; do not wait on another commit's run.\n\nFor a pull request, wait for every reported check:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ pr: { waitForChecks } }, input: { number: number; repo: string }) =>\n waitForChecks({ ...input, raise: true })\n```\n\nInspect the returned commit identity, outcome, and merge state; a fulfilled request is not evidence that CI passed: check `outcome`, which is `\"passed\"`, `\"failed\"` (returned only with `raise: false`), or `\"pending\"`. `ci.waitForCommit()` repeats its run's `outcome` and `conclusion` at the top level. To compare durations, such as before and after a CI change or cold and warm native builds, time the exact run:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ ci: { inspectTimings } }, input: { repo: string; id: number }) =>\n inspectTimings({ ...input, steps: \"^(Build|Test)\" })\n```\n\nWhen a run fails, call `ci.inspectFailure({ repo, id })` and read its excerpts before changing the workflow or rerunning it. For test jobs, `testFailures` lists each failed Vitest test with its first error line and `testSummary` holds Vitest's totals; `testFailuresOmitted` counts failures that the list or the fetched log window did not include. Distinguish timeouts from assertion failures before deciding whether a change or the runner is at fault.\n\nA wait that times out is not a failure: long CI and release runs can outlast one 285 s budget, so every wait returns `outcome: \"pending\"` with a `note` and a `hint` instead of throwing, even with `raise: true`. Follow the hint: call `pr.waitForChecks()` again, or pass the discovered run ID to `ci.waitForRun()` instead of rediscovering. Start each wait only after the merge, push, or discovery result that supplies its SHA or run ID has returned.\n\nRecord verified outcomes in the pull request description with `pr.editBody()`. It replaces exact text, ticks `- [ ]` items, and appends sections, but writes nothing when an expected text is missing or ambiguous; a stale checklist is a signal to re-read the description, not to loosen the expectation. Preview with `dryRun: true`:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ pr: { editBody } }, input: { number: number; repo: string; check: string[] }) =>\n editBody({ ...input, dryRun: true })\n```\n\n## Open and merge pull requests\n\nAfter commit/push authorization, `delivery.openPullRequest()` creates the branch from the current HEAD (uncommitted changes move with it), commits and pushes the listed files through `delivery.commit()`, and opens the pull request, or returns the branch's open one. It reuses the branch when it is already checked out:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync (\n { delivery: { openPullRequest } },\n input: { branch: string; files: string[]; message: string; body: string },\n) => openPullRequest(input)\n```\n\nAfter merge authorization and passing checks, `pr.merge()` merges an open pull request. With `sync: true` it then switches to the base branch and runs `git pull --ff-only`; a failed sync returns `synced.ok: false` with the failing step, since the merge already happened:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ pr: { merge } }, input: { number: number }) =>\n merge({ ...input, method: \"squash\", sync: true })\n```\n\n## Finish an issue\n\nFor non-interactive changes:\n\n1. Validate.\n2. Prepare delivery.\n3. Commit with tests and the closing keyword.\n4. Push, verify the exact CI run, update the epic, and confirm a clean synchronized worktree.\n\nFor TUI, extension, reload, saved-function, sandbox, progress, or renderer behavior:\n\n1. Validate and prepare delivery.\n2. Commit and push **without** `Closes #...`.\n3. Ask the user to run `/reload`. That reloads only the Pit that Pi loaded. If Pi loads Pit from an installed package, which shows as `~/.pi/agent/git/github.com/cv/pit` in place of the checkout, ask the user to restart Pi from the checkout instead: `pi -ne -e ./src/index.ts --session <sessionFile>`. `-ne` stops the installed copy from loading as well.\n4. Exercise live partial state and expanded final state interactively.\n5. Test relevant success, warning, failure, concurrency, nesting, cancellation, or timeout cases.\n6. Correct observed mismatches and revalidate.\n7. Make the final closing commit only after observed acceptance.\n8. Push, verify the exact CI run, update the epic, and confirm a clean synchronized worktree.\n\n## Release\n\nFollow [releasing.md](../../../docs/releasing.md). `main` is protected, so the version bump lands through a `release-X.Y.Z` pull request like any other change. Tag the resulting `main` commit only after its CI passes.\n\nAfter the Release workflow succeeds, verify what it published before declaring delivery complete. `release.verifyPublished()` checks the tag commit, that the release has no assets, and an install from a fresh tag clone that runs the sandbox, and fails with every problem it found:\n\n```ts pit-example\nasync ({ release: { verifyPublished } }, input: { tag: string }) => verifyPublished(input)\n```\n\nIt does not replace the tag smoke test in the release guide, which exercises the installed package in Pi.\n\n## Failure recovery\n\n- Gate failure: read the bounded diagnostic tail before rerunning validation.\n- Helper failure: use its structured result and bounded diagnostics before dropping to lower-level functions.\n- Anchor or revision failure: re-read; do not guess another anchor.\n- TypeScript tool syntax failure: move content to params and reduce nesting.\n- Two failures of one class: stop varying syntax and split the workflow.\n- Truncated machine output: aggregate in the function before parsing it.\n", "refs": { "entries": [ ".pi/skills/pit-delivery", ".pi/skills/pit-delivery/SKILL.md" ], "truncated": false } }

pr.title: feat(durable): collapse finished runs' tool calls to their labels after each run
pr.body:
Refs #396. Acceptance needs a release and a live pi-action thread, so this PR doesn't close the issue.

## What it does

After every run that answers, pi-durable hosts collapse the tool calls of older finished runs into one deterministic line each. No model call is involved. The line is written in the same `afterRun` write that applies the edits the model staged during the run, so there's still a single `pit.context-edit` entry per run:

```
[Pit: collapsed typescript call · "Read npm and git global and command sources" · workspace.read, workspace.search · ok · ~18.2K tokens · originals: session.inspectEntry("212"), session.inspectEntry("213")]
```

- **Label:** the `// @pit:` header or the `label` argument, else the program's first line, resolved the same way as `present.call`. The functions come from the same parsing `present.result` uses. The outcome is `ok`, `failed: <error's first line>`, `asked: <title>`, `saved <name>`, or `no result`. For other tools the line gives the tool name and the outcome. An entry with several calls lists each one, separated by `;`.
- **Shape:** the assistant entry keeps its text and thinking, signatures included. Its tool calls become the line and its results are omitted, so no call is left unanswered and no result is orphaned. The pairing is the same as `elide`.
- **Never touched:** user and host messages, answers, compaction summaries, notes, entries already rewritten or with a staged edit, entries no larger than their line, and the current run. A model `elide` or `summarize` staged in the same run wins, and the collapse skips its targets.
- **Provenance:** `operation: "collapse"` sits next to the model's `elide`/`summarize` operations. `session.outline()` shows collapsed entries as `elided`, with the line as the preview. I didn't add a new outline state, because `PitContextState` is shared with Pi's global contract. `inspectEntry` still returns every original.
- **Runs:** a run starts at the user or host messages that follow the previous run's entries. Everything from `run.first` onward is the current run. The view is read from the active range in the same commit, so the collapse never crosses the newest compaction head, and a fork keeps the view it had at its fork point.
- **Guideline:** when collapse is on, `pit_guidelines` gains this line: "Calls from finished runs collapse to their labels: give each call a specific label, and say in your answer what a later run will need."

## Defaults (a behaviour change, listed in CHANGELOG)

- **On by default:** `collapse: { keepRuns: 1, minTokens: 32_000 }`. pi-action is the main durable host and runs headless, so nobody follows Pit's context-pressure notices there. `collapse: false` turns it off.
- **`keepRuns: 1`** counts the run that just answered. The follow-up usually refers to that run, so it stays whole and older runs collapse.
- **`minTokens: 32_000`** counts the conversation's messages only, not the system prompt, tools, and sections. On pi-action those fixed parts are about 41K tokens, so a floor on the whole context would always be exceeded. Below about 32K the transcript is smaller than the fixed prompt, so collapsing would cut a cold follow-up by less than half while losing verbatim history. Above it the transcript dominates. Thread #383's 170K prompt was far past it.

## Line bound

Each line is at most 512 bytes. Labels and outcomes are first cut to 160 characters each. If the line is still too long, the injected function list goes first, then the description is cut at its end with `…`. The token size and the `inspectEntry` IDs are never cut. When the usual form doesn't fit, the IDs switch to `session.inspectEntry(id) for "212", "213"`. An entry with so many parallel calls that its IDs alone pass 512 bytes keeps all its IDs and names no calls.

## Strict-provider check

I ran this with pi-ai's `anthropic-messages` API against `aws/anthropic/bedrock-claude-opus-5-5` on `https://inference-api.nvidia.com`, the route pi-action uses, with adaptive thinking:

- **Accepted:** user, then two collapsed tool-calling turns in a row (each `thinking` with its real signature + `text` + collapsed line, `stopReason: stop`), then the answer, then a follow-up. That's three assistant messages in a row. Also accepted: the same without thinking, and a later run's live tool call and result after a collapsed run. So I kept the issue's shape and did not merge adjacent assistant messages.
- **With the guideline** in the system prompt, the model read the lines as its earlier calls: "it called echo twice: the transcript shows two collapsed echo-call markers, both marked ok…".
- **Without the guideline**, the model once said a collapsed line was "text I wrote myself". That's the reason the guideline ships with the feature.
- **Rejected:** sending the *same* signed thinking block twice, which I did only as an artificial copy. The request was blocked as "duplicating model outputs". The collapse never copies a block, because each entry keeps its own thinking.

`docs/durable.md` records this.

## Tests

The integration tests use the real pi-durable harness in `test/durable/context.test.ts` and check what the model sees next:

- Three runs with `keepRuns: 1`: the first two runs' calls are collapsed lines; the third run's call, every answer, and every user message are verbatim; calls stay paired. A fork taken before the third run keeps its second run whole. `inspectEntry` returns each original. A fourth run collapses only the third, so no entry is collapsed twice.
- `minTokens` above the context size, and `collapse: false`: nothing collapses, no edit entry is written, and the guideline appears only when collapse is on.
- A failed run (the harness gained `run(…, { fail: true })`): nothing collapses and its staged elide drops.
- A model elide staged in the same run, with `keepRuns: 2`: one entry with operations `["elide", "collapse"]`, the elided call left to the model, the sibling call collapsed, and the kept run whole.

The planning tests in `test/durable/context-planning.test.ts`:

- A line-format table: labelled, unlabelled (first line), failed (error's first line), failed with no text, another tool, several calls and results, missing result, a posted question, and `saveOnly`.
- The byte bound, including multibyte labels, the short ID form, and an IDs-only line.
- The `keepRuns` boundary table; the compaction head; thinking and text kept; and an entry its line wouldn't shrink.

`tests.probeMutation`:

- **`keepRuns` off by one** (`runs.length - (keepRuns - 1)` → `runs.length - keepRuns`): killed by the line table and the run-boundary tests.
- **Inputs no longer start runs:** killed by the `keepRuns: 2` boundary row and the elide-plus-collapse integration test.
- **Answers treated as candidates** (dropping `toolCallIds.length === 0`): survives. The collapse always keeps an entry's text, so an entry without calls can never shrink and the size check leaves it. Answers stay protected even under this mutation, and the tests that assert answers are verbatim still pass. User messages have two guards as well: the assistant-role check and `protectedReason`.

`delivery.validate({ coverage: true, packageCheck: true })` passes: check, tests, coverage, and package.

## Acceptance (after merge)

- [ ] Release, and point pi-assistant at the new tag
- [ ] On a pi-action thread with at least two earlier runs, the follow-up's stored entries and `session.outline()` show the older runs' calls collapsed, and the first prompt is much smaller
- [ ] The provider accepts the collapsed context live
- [ ] `session.inspectEntry` recovers a collapsed result when the follow-up needs it

Pi (`src/context/`) is untouched.

value.skill:
---
name: pit-delivery
description: Implements and delivers Pit issues by orchestrating trusted project functions for bounded review, validation, CI, reload, interactive smoke testing, and issue closure. Use for Pit feature, refactor, release, and issue-finalization work.
---

# Pit delivery

## Operating model

This skill owns workflow policy: sequencing, judgment, acceptance criteria, and recovery. Trusted project functions own repeatable execution and bounded result shaping.

- Call an existing project helper by name instead of recreating its internal npm, Git, GitHub, coverage, or session-analysis workflow.
- Compose helpers when a phase needs more than one operation, but keep dependent mutations serialized.
- Do not create a same-named session override for a project helper during delivery.
- If a helper is unexpectedly unavailable, inspect `context.get()` and `functions.getSaved(name)`. Repair the trusted project configuration or helper rather than silently maintaining a duplicate workflow in this skill.
- If helper behavior must change, update its file under `.pi/functions/` and its tests; keep this skill focused on when and why to invoke it.
- When adding, promoting, renaming, or changing a helper, review its owning skill's trigger, preconditions, result interpretation, and recovery path in the same change. Do not create another registry or copy every function into every skill.
- Editing a helper file does not refresh the active definition. `functions.getSaved(name)` describes the loaded definition; disk-based tests describe the file. After helper edits, use `/reload`, inspect the effective scope/override chain, and smoke-test the changed behavior before claiming live acceptance. Reload also refreshes changed skills and prompt templates.

## Implement

1. Read the issue, parent epic, and relevant comments.
2. Inspect current architecture and tests before editing. When writing, changing, or reviewing tests, load [pit-test-audit](../pit-test-audit/SKILL.md) and apply its authoring gate. For renderer, progress, diagnostic, or presentation-data changes, load [pit-terminal-ux](../pit-terminal-ux/SKILL.md) and use its design and acceptance criteria throughout the work.
3. Use fresh hashed anchors for every mutation. Re-read after edits and formatting.
4. Use top-level params for multiline patches. Simplify immediately after a malformed submission.
5. Prefer typed npm, Git, and GitHub functions for one-off operations not covered by a project helper. Use raw CLI only for unsupported operations.
6. Batch independent reads and probes, but serialize mutations and dependent transitions.

## Choose project helpers

Use only helpers relevant to the current phase. Discover names and signatures with `functions.listAll({ scope: "project", limit: 20 })`, following `nextOffset` as needed, and inspect relevant definitions with `functions.getSaved(name)`. Use `Promise.allSettled` for optional availability probes so a missing helper does not hide the other diagnostics.

Blocks marked `ts pit-example` are complete tool programs checked against the project registry by the resource tests. They are not executed by those tests. Supply the second argument through tool `params`; examples do not authorize their effects.

For a focused test run:

```ts pit-example
async ({ tests: { runTargeted } }, input: { files: string[]; testNamePattern?: string }) =>
  runTargeted({ ...input, slowest: 5 })
```

- Use `tests.runTargeted()` during the implementation loop, not the full suite after every edit.
- `tests.runTargeted()` reports failures from Vitest's JSON report. Add `testNamePattern` to rerun one case and `slowest` to measure where time goes.
- Use `delivery.commit()` only after commit/push authorization. It stages exactly the listed files, refuses unrelated staged changes, and can push the branch. Validation or a skill invocation is not permission to publish.
- Use `delivery.review()` before validation and after substantial corrections.
- Use `tests.inspectCoverageGaps()` after coverage has generated its HTML report.
- Use `delivery.auditCodeQuality()` for broad feature or refactor work where maintainability risk matters.
- `delivery.format()` formats only changed supported files and invalidates their anchors. Re-read every written file before another mutation. It cannot see committed files, so run it after the last edit and before `delivery.commit()`.
- `delivery.validate()` and `delivery.prepare()` first check that installed direct dependencies match `package-lock.json`. A stale install fails validation before any gate runs, with each package's declared, locked, and installed versions. Run `npm ci` (or `npm install` after editing `package.json`). Pass `dependencies: false` only for an intentional local override.
- Use `sessions.analyze()` for one session and `sessions.analyzeRecent()` for project-wide workflow trends. To judge a prompt template or skill by its real use, `sessions.findPromptRuns({ marker })` finds its past runs in every project's sessions by the text its expanded message starts with, and reports what each run did, what it cost, and the user's next message. Repeated follow-ups such as "commit" or "continue" point at what the prompt left undone. These diagnose agent workflow; they do not replace code validation.
- To judge a context or prompt change by its real cost, read `context.cache`. It attributes each request's prompt-cache writes to a cause: steady growth, a context edit, a system-prompt update, an idle expiry during a run or between turns, a compaction, a model change, or something else. `contextEdits` sets Pit's re-prefill estimate against what providers rewrote. `rewritten` counts cached tokens written again; dollars appear only when Pi recorded a cost for the model. Pass `cacheLifetimeSeconds` when the provider's cache outlives or expires before the default 300 s; `longestHitGapSeconds` shows the longest observed gap that still hit.

When every change in the worktree belongs to one commit, include deletions from the listing instead of adding deleted paths by hand:

```ts pit-example
async ({ delivery: { listChangedFiles, commit } }, input: { message: string }) =>
  commit({ files: (await listChangedFiles({ includeDeleted: true })).files, message: input.message })
```

For pull-request work, inspect bounded metadata first:

```ts pit-example
async ({ pr: { inspect } }, input: { number: number; repo?: string }) =>
  inspect(input)
```

When an isolated checkout is needed, use `pr.manageWorktree({ action: "create", number })`. Always remove the temporary review worktree with its returned path through `pr.manageWorktree({ action: "remove", path })` after review.

### Diagnose dependency-related failures

For missing package APIs, unexpected installed versions, or a recently changed lockfile, inspect before reinstalling or changing source:

```ts pit-example
async ({ delivery: { inspectDependencies } }) =>
  inspectDependencies({ packages: ["@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent", "@earendil-works/pi-tui", "vitest"] })
```

Read the per-package `issues`, `lockError`, `complete`, and `omitted` fields. `matchesLock: null` means unknown/incomplete, not healthy; narrow the selection or resolve unreadable metadata. `false` calls for diagnosing the reported mismatch, not an automatic install. `true` only compares the selected direct dependencies' metadata/versions with the lockfile; it does not prove semver compatibility, package contents, or unrelated dependencies. Missing optional packages may be intentional.

If synchronization is justified and authorized, use the repository's lockfile-preserving install workflow, then rerun the affected checks. Keep platform-dependent fixture failures distinct from dependency drift and product regressions.

## Validate

Invoke the trusted project function once:

```ts pit-example
async ({ delivery: { validate } }) => validate({ coverage: true, packageCheck: true })
```

It runs check and tests together, then coverage, then package verification. A failed gate includes a bounded diagnostic tail. Read that output before rerunning a gate. Do not separately rerun completed gates or run full tests and coverage concurrently.

Before delivery, inspect Git readiness without repeating validation:

```ts pit-example
async ({ delivery: { prepare } }) => prepare()
```

`ready: true` means Git inspection and whitespace checks passed. It does not mean the worktree is clean, tests/CI passed, publication is authorized, or interactive acceptance happened. Review the returned Git status and both diff checks. Similarly, `delivery.format({ checkOnly: true })` returning `formatted: false` is a failed formatting check, not successful no-op work. Format only changed files. If delivery preparation exposes a change, correct it and rerun only the affected inner-loop checks before one final validation.

## Verify CI

After pushing, use the existing discovery/wait composition for the exact commit, not the newest unrelated run. Give waiting tool invocations a 300000 ms timeout; a helper's polling budget does not extend the outer tool timeout.

```ts pit-example
async ({ ci: { waitForCommit } }, input: { repo: string; sha: string }) =>
  waitForCommit({ ...input, runName: "ci.yml", raise: true })
```

Use `ci.findRun()` alone when only discovery is needed, or `ci.waitForRun()` when the exact run ID is already known. A missing run is a synchronization/trigger problem; do not wait on another commit's run.

For a pull request, wait for every reported check:

```ts pit-example
async ({ pr: { waitForChecks } }, input: { number: number; repo: string }) =>
  waitForChecks({ ...input, raise: true })
```

Inspect the returned commit identity, outcome, and merge state; a fulfilled request is not evidence that CI passed: check `outcome`, which is `"passed"`, `"failed"` (returned only with `raise: false`), or `"pending"`. `ci.waitForCommit()` repeats its run's `outcome` and `conclusion` at the top level. To compare durations, such as before and after a CI change or cold and warm native builds, time the exact run:

```ts pit-example
async ({ ci: { inspectTimings } }, input: { repo: string; id: number }) =>
  inspectTimings({ ...input, steps: "^(Build|Test)" })
```

When a run fails, call `ci.inspectFailure({ repo, id })` and read its excerpts before changing the workflow or rerunning it. For test jobs, `testFailures` lists each failed Vitest test with its first error line and `testSummary` holds Vitest's totals; `testFailuresOmitted` counts failures that the list or the fetched log window did not include. Distinguish timeouts from assertion failures before deciding whether a change or the runner is at fault.

A wait that times out is not a failure: long CI and release runs can outlast one 285 s budget, so every wait returns `outcome: "pending"` with a `note` and a `hint` instead of throwing, even with `raise: true`. Follow the hint: call `pr.waitForChecks()` again, or pass the discovered run ID to `ci.waitForRun()` instead of rediscovering. Start each wait only after the merge, push, or discovery result that supplies its SHA or run ID has returned.

Record verified outcomes in the pull request description with `pr.editBody()`. It replaces exact text, ticks `- [ ]` items, and appends sections, but writes nothing when an expected text is missing or ambiguous; a stale checklist is a signal to re-read the description, not to loosen the expectation. Preview with `dryRun: true`:

```ts pit-example
async ({ pr: { editBody } }, input: { number: number; repo: string; check: string[] }) =>
  editBody({ ...input, dryRun: true })
```

## Open and merge pull requests

After commit/push authorization, `delivery.openPullRequest()` creates the branch from the current HEAD (uncommitted changes move with it), commits and pushes the listed files through `delivery.commit()`, and opens the pull request, or returns the branch's open one. It reuses the branch when it is already checked out:

```ts pit-example
async (
  { delivery: { openPullRequest } },
  input: { branch: string; files: string[]; message: string; body: string },
) => openPullRequest(input)
```

After merge authorization and passing checks, `pr.merge()` merges an open pull request. With `sync: true` it then switches to the base branch and runs `git pull --ff-only`; a failed sync returns `synced.ok: false` with the failing step, since the merge already happened:

```ts pit-example
async ({ pr: { merge } }, input: { number: number }) =>
  merge({ ...input, method: "squash", sync: true })
```

## Finish an issue

For non-interactive changes:

1. Validate.
2. Prepare delivery.
3. Commit with tests and the closing keyword.
4. Push, verify the exact CI run, update the epic, and confirm a clean synchronized worktree.

For TUI, extension, reload, saved-function, sandbox, progress, or renderer behavior:

1. Validate and prepare delivery.
2. Commit and push **without** `Closes #...`.
3. Ask the user to run `/reload`. That reloads only the Pit that Pi loaded. If Pi loads Pit from an installed package, which shows as `~/.pi/agent/git/github.com/cv/pit` in place of the checkout, ask the user to restart Pi from the checkout instead: `pi -ne -e ./src/index.ts --session <sessionFile>`. `-ne` stops the installed copy from loading as well.
4. Exercise live partial state and expanded final state interactively.
5. Test relevant success, warning, failure, concurrency, nesting, cancellation, or timeout cases.
6. Correct observed mismatches and revalidate.
7. Make the final closing commit only after observed acceptance.
8. Push, verify the exact CI run, update the epic, and confirm a clean synchronized worktree.

## Release

Follow [releasing.md](../../../docs/releasing.md). `main` is protected, so the version bump lands through a `release-X.Y.Z` pull request like any other change. Tag the resulting `main` commit only after its CI passes.

After the Release workflow succeeds, verify what it published before declaring delivery complete. `release.verifyPublished()` checks the tag commit, that the release has no assets, and an install from a fresh tag clone that runs the sandbox, and fails with every problem it found:

```ts pit-example
async ({ release: { verifyPublished } }, input: { tag: string }) => verifyPublished(input)
```

It does not replace the tag smoke test in the release guide, which exercises the installed package in Pi.

## Failure recovery

- Gate failure: read the bounded diagnostic tail before rerunning validation.
- Helper failure: use its structured result and bounded diagnostics before dropping to lower-level functions.
- Anchor or revision failure: re-read; do not guess another anchor.
- TypeScript tool syntax failure: move content to params and reduce nesting.
- Two failures of one class: stop varying syntax and split the workflow.
- Truncated machine output: aggregate in the function before parsing it.
